data.title: Range Rover Electric explained: Why it took 11 years to bring this luxurious electric SUV to production
data.description:
A decade ago, the idea of a fully electric Range Rover might have seemed as likely as, well, a flying car – at least partly because it would have been impossible to build one with enough range to get to the end of a typical owner’s country driveway.

And yet the brand’s global boss, Martin Limpert, swears the decision to create one was made, and the work begun, 11 years ago. And that it was driven, even then, by customer demand.

“We are not so much driven by legislation, so that was not the reason we did this — although there are markets where the taxation schemes are supporting the electrification journey — but it was more about customer demand,” Limpert said.

“But the main reason was that it’s the natural fit for Range Rover. Everything the brand stands for — being quiet, calm, effortless, refined, and still capable — we just know that the electric propulsion system enhances all of this.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared


READ MORE: Range Rover Sport Electric priced for Australia: Two models starting from $226,518
READ MORE: Range Rover Electric finally revealed: $317,718 luxury EV packs 405kW, 535km real-world range and 350kW charging
READ MORE: Hot stuff: Orders open for 2025 Range Rover Electric as luxury SUV enters final testing phase

“So when we set out 11 years ago with the architecture we have now, we always knew the flexible architecture would allow us to build an electric propulsion.”

What followed, of course, was a huge amount of expense — arguably so much that the brand couldn’t afford to make its Electric Range Rover look any different to its ICE ones.

The big reason for the spending was that Range Rover was not happy with any of the electric motor or battery technology available, and decided to develop its own batteries and electric drive units in the UK — to be sure it met its needs for packaging, energy density, off-road ability and the ability to tow 2.5 tonnes.

In terms of the range a Range Rover owner requires, Limpert says the company analysed travel data from more than two million existing customers, which showed that one charge of the new car’s 118.5kWh battery will cover 97 per cent of their ordinary journeys.

The car’s WLTP range is 609km, but Limpert is unusually willing to dismiss that as a notional, laboratory figure and is happy, instead, to defend what he calls the Range Rover’s real-world range of 535km.

In the UK, and some other markets, Limpert says the brand has also worked hard to make charging effortless for its customers, with a single RFID card that works with every major fast-charging network. Owners tap the card on the charger, plug in and charge, with no app or credit card required.

Limpert said Range Rover has a provider in Australia, which should ease a common local frustration, but it remains to be seen whether the brand can get all charging companies on board to what sounds like a fantastic idea.

Limpert says demand has been strong for the Range Rover Electric already, with around 70 per cent of people on the waiting list new to the brand, many of whom are already driving EVs and reluctant to go back.

Limpert believes electric power lifts the Range Rover experience: the cabin is about 7 decibels quieter, torque distribution is 100 times faster than in current models, while the sealed battery and drive units allow 900mm wading depth.

Personally, he’s been driving both the new car and his old, ICE Autobiography version, and he says he prefers the Electric version, which will cost well north of $300,000 when it arrives in Australia early next year.

Watch out for Stephen Corby’s first drive of the Range Rover Electric. Coming this weekend.

The post Range Rover Electric explained: Why it took 11 years to bring this luxurious electric SUV to production appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: New research: Cheaper EVs tipped to cushion FBT cuts as overseas markets offer a warning
data.description:
Australia’s growing choice of electric cars priced below $75,000 could help prevent a sales slump when the federal government starts winding back its fringe benefits tax exemption, according to the salary packaging industry.

The National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association says the first stage of the changes, scheduled for April 2027, is unlikely to materially affect demand because most Australian EV buyers already choose vehicles below the new threshold.

Its assessment comes as finance broker Savvy highlights falls in electric vehicle market share overseas after purchase incentives were withdrawn.

READ MORE: Best EVs to buy in Australia 2026: The ultimate guide to affordable electric cars at every price

READ MORE: Unplugged! EV FBT buying incentives to be reduced as sales spiral. Not everyone is happy
READ MORE: TV campaign to save the FBT tax exemption launches: EV sales at stake warn backers
READ MORE: Thinking of taking out a novated lease to buy a new EV so you can leverage the fringe benefits tax exemption? Read this first

However, the overseas experience does not provide a direct forecast for Australia, where support is being reduced in stages rather than removed outright.

“We believe the changes to the Electric Car Discount from April 2027 won’t have a material impact on sales because most Australians are buying EVs priced below the $75,000 threshold, and a majority of EVs in Australia sit below this price point,” NALSPA chief executive Rohan Martin said in the Savvy release.

Under the government’s announced changes, eligible EVs valued above $75,000 will move from a full FBT exemption to a 25 per cent discount for new commitments from April 1, 2027, subject to the applicable luxury car tax eligibility limit.

Eligible EVs valued at $75,000 or less will retain the full exemption for commitments made before April 1, 2029. New eligible commitments from that date will receive the smaller 25 per cent discount regardless of vehicle value.

A 25 per cent discount means three-quarters of the otherwise applicable FBT remains payable. It does not mean a 25 per cent reduction in the price of the car.

Treasury released draft legislation for consultation in September. The proposed transition is tied to commitments to provide a vehicle, so the dates should not be interpreted as automatically ending the exemption on every existing lease.

The current exemption applies to eligible employer-provided electric cars, including those supplied through salary packaging arrangements known as novated leases. It is not a rebate available to everyone buying an EV with cash or a conventional car loan.

Martin said more than half of new battery electric vehicles sold in Australia were acquired through novated leasing supported by the discount. That is the industry association’s estimate.

Savvy Benefits general manager Adrian Taylor said the wider range of affordable vehicles should help soften the changes.

“The main difference between EV sales now and a few years ago is that there’s now far more vehicles to pick from. The incentive changes will have less of an impact now as there’s far more EVs below $75,000,” he said.

Both organisations have an interest in the policy: NALSPA represents leasing and salary packaging providers, while Savvy offers novated leasing among its financial services.

Overseas figures nevertheless show why the industry is watching the transition closely.

In Germany, battery electric cars accounted for 13.5 per cent of new passenger car registrations in 2024, down from 18.4 per cent in 2023. Registrations fell 27.4 per cent to 380,609 vehicles.

That followed the closure of Germany’s environmental bonus scheme to new applications in December 2023.

Canada also experienced a decline after its federal purchase incentive program ran out of funding and was paused in January 2025. Transport Canada’s dashboard puts battery electric vehicles at 6.7 per cent of new light-duty registrations in 2025, down from 11.4 per cent in 2024.

Transport Canada’s figures also show a partial recovery to 8.0 per cent in the first quarter of 2026.

New Zealand also ended its Clean Car Discount on December 31, 2023, although differences in market coverage and other policy changes complicate comparisons with Australia.

Falls in market share should not be confused with equivalent falls in sales volumes, and changes in incentives are not the only influence on demand. Vehicle availability, prices, broader economic conditions and purchases brought forward ahead of a deadline can all affect the comparison.

For Australia, retaining the full exemption on cheaper EVs should limit the immediate exposure in 2027. The broader test comes in 2029, when new eligible arrangements below $75,000 also move to the smaller concession.

“We believe the Federal Government has taken a sensible approach by phasing the discount gradually to prevent demand from stalling,” Martin said.

For buyers, the tax benefit remains only one part of the calculation. As EV Central has previously reported, finance rates, fees, insurance costs and the residual payment also need to be considered when comparing a novated lease with other ways of buying an electric car.

The post New research: Cheaper EVs tipped to cushion FBT cuts as overseas markets offer a warning appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh
data.description:
Electric car makers have increasingly turned to bigger batteries to deliver longer driving ranges, but Volkswagen’s remarkable Mission Efficiency prototype demonstrates there’s another way.

The German brand’s ultra-slippery experimental EV has recorded average energy consumption of just 6.89kWh/100km during a 1278km European road trip, despite carrying a relatively modest 54.9kWh usable battery.

For some perspective, plenty of contemporary electric cars consume somewhere in the teens of kWh/100km, while larger and heavier electric SUVs can easily venture beyond 20kWh/100km.

READ MORE: 6.48kWh/100km! Volkswagen Mission Efficiency electric car shows how frugal an EV can be in the real world
READ MORE: Global unveiling: After many teases, the VW ID. Polo has been revealed in full. Is this the best small EV in the world?
READ MORE: Volkswagen turns iconic GTI on its head: Electric ID.3 is first rear-drive GTI and the most powerful ever

Volkswagen’s answer isn’t one breakthrough technology. Instead, it has attacked virtually everything that consumes or wastes energy, from aerodynamics and tyre resistance to braking, weight, climate control and even the stereo.

And much of what sits underneath the Mission Efficiency isn’t experimental.

Its 99kW front-mounted electric motor and battery are derived from the technology developed for the new Volkswagen ID. Polo, while the underlying front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture will underpin a new generation of relatively affordable Volkswagen EVs.

That makes the Mission Efficiency an intriguing demonstration of how much further an EV might travel if engineers concentrate on reducing its energy requirement rather than simply adding more battery.

Aerodynamics

The Mission Efficiency’s most spectacular number is its drag coefficient of just 0.158.

But drag coefficient is only part of the equation. The VW also has a small frontal area of 2.08 square metres, helped by its unusually low 1392mm overall height.

Its body then progressively narrows towards the rear in the classic aerodynamic teardrop or ‘boat-tail’ shape.

Volkswagen has attacked the airflow in less obvious places too.

The underbody is almost completely enclosed, the rear wheels are covered and three active cooling flaps in the nose remain closed when cooling air isn’t required.

The doors use frameless windows and flush handles, while the rear axle has even been narrowed compared with the ID. Polo to help clean up airflow beneath the car.

The benefits increase dramatically with speed because aerodynamic drag becomes an increasingly important component of a vehicle’s total energy requirement.

Volkswagen claims the Mission Efficiency consumes more than 30 per cent less energy than an ID. Polo once speeds exceed 80km/h.

The most telling comparison comes at German autobahn speeds: VW says driving the Mission Efficiency at about 140km/h requires roughly the same amount of energy as driving an ID. Polo at 100km/h.

Wheels

One of the more fascinating lessons from the project concerns wheels.

Volkswagen estimates they are responsible for between 25 and 30 per cent of a vehicle’s aerodynamic resistance.

So rather than simply fitting conventional aero wheel covers, its engineers worked on controlling airflow both around and through them.

The front wheelarches sit closely around the tyres to reduce turbulence, while the rear wheels are completely enclosed.

VW has also developed patented deflectors mounted on the inside of all four wheels. Their job is to prevent air entering the rims and creating turbulence. Flat external wheel covers complete the package.

Then there are the tyres themselves. Volkswagen worked with Continental to develop special tyres based on its production EcoContact 7.

Their claimed rolling resistance is just 4.9kg per tonne, around 25 per cent below the threshold required to achieve the European Union’s highest Class A tyre rating.

Battery

Mission Efficiency’s battery is particularly interesting because its capacity is nothing extraordinary. It contains 54.9kWh of usable energy – less than many mainstream EVs.

It uses NMC lithium-ion chemistry and cell-to-pack construction, eliminating conventional intermediate battery modules by integrating cells more directly into the pack.

The battery is related to the production unit developed for the ID. Polo, although Volkswagen unlocked an additional 2.9kWh of usable capacity through software for Mission Efficiency.

Maximum DC charging power is 105kW and AC charging is rated at 11kW. Those aren’t headline-grabbing charging figures. The point is that Mission Efficiency needs relatively little electricity in the first place.

Its official WLTP energy consumption is just 8.4kWh/100km. During Volkswagen’s documented 1278.36km journey from Wolfsburg in Germany to Vienna in Austria, that fell to 6.89kWh/100km excluding charging losses, or 7.51kWh/100km when those losses were included.

The battery required only one recharge during the journey and VW says the car arrived with another 164km of indicated range remaining.

A separate idealised test at a constant 68km/h, without gradients and with energy consumers such as air-conditioning switched off, produced an even lower 6.48kWh/100km.

Braking

Another potential pointer towards future production EVs is hidden in the braking system.

Mission Efficiency retains conventional hydraulic brakes at the front but uses a new electromechanical brake at the rear, developed jointly by Volkswagen and automotive technology company Aumovio.

Rather than hydraulic pressure activating the rear brakes, electrical actuators do the job. That eliminates rear hydraulic lines and brake fluid while reducing mechanical friction losses.

More importantly for an EV, Volkswagen says the system enables variable brake-force distribution and can improve the interaction between friction braking and regenerative braking.

That potentially allows more of the vehicle’s kinetic energy to be recovered and returned to the battery rather than disappearing as heat through the brakes.

Solar

There is also a 370-watt photovoltaic system integrated into the glass roof and rear section of the Mission Efficiency.

Volkswagen says it can contribute the equivalent of up to 30km of extra range per day, depending heavily on location, weather and season.

But that needs some qualification. The solar cells aren’t intended to transform Mission Efficiency into a solar-powered EV. They feed the vehicle’s electrical system and reduce the amount of energy ancillary systems need to draw from the traction battery.

It’s another example of the philosophy behind the entire car: rather than finding one enormous energy saving, VW has accumulated lots of smaller ones.

Air-conditioning

Climate control can take a significant bite out of an EV’s available energy, particularly when heating the cabin in cold conditions.

Mission Efficiency therefore uses a heat pump to reduce the electrical energy required for heating. The system uses R744 – carbon dioxide – as its refrigerant rather than a conventional synthetic refrigerant.

Volkswagen has applied the same energy-saving philosophy elsewhere inside. There’s no conventional infotainment screen. Instead, occupants bring a smartphone or tablet.

Even conventional permanently installed speakers have been deleted and replaced by a portable Bluetooth speaker.

Weight

The Mission Efficiency combines elements of the ID. Polo structure with a self-supporting aluminium construction, while the doors, bonnet, tailgate, guards and other components employ carbon-fibre and aramid composite materials.

That part of the formula is clearly less representative of an affordable production EV than its motor and battery technology, because extensive lightweight composites remain expensive.

Nevertheless, it illustrates the engineering trade-off inherent in long-range EVs.

Adding battery capacity increases range, but also adds weight. That additional weight then requires more energy to accelerate and move, potentially requiring still more battery capacity.

Mission Efficiency attacks the problem from the opposite direction.

Mirrors

There’s even an interesting lesson in something Volkswagen decided not to fit.

Despite the extreme aerodynamic focus, Mission Efficiency retains conventional exterior mirrors rather than replacing them with cameras.

Volkswagen says wind-tunnel development showed the overall aerodynamic benefit from camera mirrors would have been relatively small.

They would also have added cost and consumed electricity.

It’s a tiny detail, but one that neatly sums up the project: a technology doesn’t automatically make the car more efficient simply because it looks more advanced.

What are the implications for future VW EVs?

Don’t expect an ID. Polo with covered rear wheels, carbon-fibre body panels and a Cd of 0.158. Mission Efficiency is a technology demonstrator rather than a preview of a production model.

But its significance is that the fundamental electrical hardware isn’t exotic.

The 99kW APP290 permanent-magnet motor, battery technology and front-wheel-drive MEB+ architecture have strong links with Volkswagen’s new generation of production EVs.

Other technologies – active cooling flaps, improved underbody aerodynamics, lower-resistance tyres, smarter thermal management, reduced brake drag and better wheel aerodynamics – are far more transferable to everyday cars than Mission Efficiency’s dramatic body shape suggests.

And that’s perhaps the most important lesson from the project. The industry’s EV range battle has often focused on how many kilowatt-hours can be squeezed beneath a vehicle.

Mission Efficiency demonstrates the other side of the equation. Make an electric car require substantially fewer kilowatt-hours to travel each 100km and suddenly a relatively modest battery can take you a very long way.

The post VW Mission Efficiency Deep Dive: Here’s how Volkswagen squeezed extraordinary EV range from just 54.9kWh appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Giant Avatr T09 luxury PHEV SUV makes world debut: Expected to join Chinese luxury newcomer’s Aussie line-up
data.description:
Chinese luxury brand Avatr has unveiled its imposing new T09 flagship plug-in hybrid SUV, offering a first public look at a six-seat rival to the biggest European luxury SUVs that is expected to eventually reach Australia.

The Concept T09 made its global debut at the Paris motor show, where Avatr also displayed the 06T electric shooting brake, which is already in the frame for the brand’s Australian rollout in 2027.

At more than 5.2 metres long and around two metres wide, the T09 is a full-size three-row SUV intended to establish a new flagship tier for Avatr, with six individual seats and an emphasis on passenger comfort.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

READ MORE: Chinese premium brand Avatr confirms first Aussie model: 07L electric SUV deliveries will start in 2027
READ MORE: Another Chinese auto giant is coming to Australia: Changan and luxury Avatr prepare EV and PHEV assault
READ MORE: Yep, yet another Chinese brand is coming to Australia: Luxury Avatr confirmed with its line-up of SUV and saloon EVs and range extenders.

The T09’s exterior features an unusually elaborate front grille incorporating 362 Avatr emblems, crystal-inspired headlights and a large clamshell bonnet. The design was developed under Avatr chief designer Nader Faghihzadeh, formerly of BMW, and follows themes introduced by the Vision Xpectra concept.

Inside, the concept previews an integrated three-screen dashboard and a retractable ‘Vortex’ lighting feature with 118 RGB LEDs. Avatr has shown the cabin as a luxury-focused six-seater, although final production equipment and trim details are still to be confirmed.

While Avatr has yet to publish a complete production specification sheet, Chinese government approval documents provide an indication of what is coming. They list a 71.24kWh battery supplied by CATL and two petrol-electric powertrain configurations.

One combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged petrol engine with front and rear electric motors, while the other uses a 2.0-litre turbocharged petrol engine and three electric motors. The more powerful version has been reported with a combined output exceeding 735kW, although official final performance figures have yet to be confirmed.

A Chinese government report quotes more than 400km of electric-only driving range under the optimistic CLTC cycle. That figure should not be treated as a likely Australian or WLTP result.

The production T09 is expected to launch in China before the end of 2026. Its Australian future is less certain: overseas-market availability has not been formally detailed by Avatr, although Australian industry reporting has pointed to a possible arrival in 2028.

If it comes here, the T09 would enter a growing field of large electrified luxury SUVs, including the Zeekr 9X, while also presenting an alternative to conventional high-end six- and seven-seat models such as the BMW X7 and Mercedes-Benz GLS.

Avatr’s Australian introduction is already taking shape without the T09. As EV Central has previously reported, the 07L electric SUV is scheduled to lead the brand’s local launch in the first half of 2027.

The 06T electric shooting brake, which is already on-sale in China is confirmed to follow in the second half of 2027. Its arrival will put Avatr into the same emerging electric-wagon market as the Zeekr 7GT.

The post Giant Avatr T09 luxury PHEV SUV makes world debut: Expected to join Chinese luxury newcomer’s Aussie line-up appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Another Chinese EV brand coming to Australia! Rox Motor targets late 2026 or early 2027 launch with luxury range-extender SUVs
data.description:
Chinese luxury SUV manufacturer Rox Motor is preparing to enter the Australian market, with a local launch being targeted for late 2026 or early 2027.

The emerging brand specialises in large, premium SUVs that combine electric propulsion with petrol-powered range extenders, promising substantial electric-only driving range without relying entirely on charging infrastructure.

Representatives working on Rox Motor’s international marketing are reaching out to Australian automotive media about its local launch plans, nominating late 2026 or early 2027 as the target for its arrival.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

But Rox has yet to confirm which models will be offered in Australia or who will handle distribution and servicing.

Australian pricing also remains unknown, making it difficult to establish exactly where the brand will sit against established premium SUVs.

Rox has previously signalled its interest in the market, with more than a dozen Australian trademark applications covering names including Rox, Adamas and Pole Stone.

Those filings have been reported previously, but no firm launch timing, Australian distributor or local sales arrangements have been publicly confirmed.

Rox Motor’s existing model range comprises the Rox 01 and newer Adamas, both substantial six- or seven-seat luxury SUVs with rugged, upright styling and an emphasis on passenger comfort, technology and outdoor touring.

Both models employ range-extender electric vehicle (REEV) powertrains, which use electric motors to drive the wheels while a petrol engine generates electricity to supplement the battery.

The Rox 01 and Adamas use dual electric motors producing a combined 350kW and 740Nm, providing all-wheel drive and a claimed 0-100km/h acceleration time of 5.5 seconds.

A turbocharged 1.5-litre four-cylinder petrol engine acts as the range extender, while a 56.01kWh battery provides a claimed electric-only driving range of up to 235km under WLTC testing.

The newer Adamas offers a claimed combined petrol-electric range of up to 1226km, compared with 1115km for the ROX 01, although both figures are based on laboratory testing rather than real-world driving.

The Adamas measures 5298mm long, 1985mm wide and 1856mm tall, riding on a 3010mm wheelbase.

That makes it longer than a Toyota LandCruiser 300 Series and places it in the same broad large luxury SUV category as the Land Rover Defender 130.

The Adamas also features adjustable air suspension, with Rox quoting up to 272mm of ground clearance and 770mm of water-wading capability in its raised off-road setting.

Equipment offered internationally includes six-seat configurations with individual second-row luxury seats, an optional camping-oriented tailgate kitchen system, a 270-degree awning and up to 5.7kW of combined vehicle-to-load (V2L) power output.

The Rox 01 has also attracted attention for an unusual camping accessory: a portable toilet designed to be carried in the vehicle, reinforcing the brand’s emphasis on outdoor adventures.

The combination of substantial electric driving range, luxury appointments and off-road-inspired styling could position ROX against established large SUVs including the Land Rover Defender, Toyota LandCruiser 300 Series and Lexus LX.

However, its range-extender electric powertrain would give it a different proposition from the predominantly diesel and petrol-powered vehicles currently dominating Australia’s large luxury off-road SUV segment.

It would also join a growing number of Chinese manufacturers introducing range-extender technology as an alternative to conventional battery-electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids.

While REEVs can deliver considerable electric-only range, they still rely on petrol for extended journeys and are generally classified as plug-in hybrids rather than pure battery-electric vehicles.

The post Another Chinese EV brand coming to Australia! Rox Motor targets late 2026 or early 2027 launch with luxury range-extender SUVs appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: XPeng G9L SUV Australian pricing looms: Flagship SUV targets early 2027 showroom arrival
data.description:
XPeng’s new G9L flagship SUV will reach Australian showrooms in early 2027, with both battery-electric and range-extender powertrains and a choice of six- and seven-seat layouts headed here.

The updated timing supersedes earlier expectations that the large Chinese SUV could arrive as soon as November 2026. Australian pricing and specifications are expected to be announced shortly, ahead of vehicles reaching dealerships next year.

The G9L will follow the smaller L03 SUV, which is expected to reach Australian dealerships before the end of 2026. Right-hand-drive G9L production has already commenced in China, with initial examples earmarked for Australia.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

READ MORE: 2026 XPeng G6 Long Range Review: Sharp-value Tesla Model Y rival does little wrong, but needs more spark
READ MORE: XPeng L03 lands in Australia from $41,900: New EV and range-extender SUV takes on Chinese price-fighters
READ MORE: XPeng X9 Aussie price and equipment: Super-smart electric seven-seater arrives to take on luxury SUVs and a new wave of high-tech people-movers

The latest developments follow the G9L’s European presentation at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, where XPeng outlined its electric powertrain, charging capabilities and premium positioning. The vehicle was originally unveiled in China earlier in the year.

European pricing starts at €74,990, although that is not a reliable guide to Australian pricing. A starting price below $100,000 is expected, but no Australian figure has been confirmed.

The price will be especially important under Australia’s changing electric-car fringe benefits tax (FBT) arrangements: from April 2027, eligible EVs below $75,000 retain the full exemption, while those priced from $75,000 to $91,000 receive a reduced 25 per cent discount.

Measuring 5120mm long and 1999mm wide, with a 3100mm wheelbase, the G9L is a substantial SUV. Six-seat versions use individual second-row chairs, while seven-seat models offer a more conventional family layout. Both configurations are expected to be available locally, although the grade structure is not yet known.

The G9L’s battery-electric versions use an 800-volt electrical architecture and offer rear- or all-wheel drive. European information indicates a maximum WLTP driving range of up to 591km, while XPeng claims a 10-80 per cent DC recharge in as little as 11.7 minutes using suitable high-powered equipment.

The range-extender version uses a petrol engine as a generator to replenish its battery, rather than driving the wheels directly. Chinese-market specifications include a 63.3kWh battery and claimed electric-only and combined ranges of up to 435km and 1602km respectively under the optimistic CLTC cycle. Those figures should not be taken as Australian-certified ranges.

It is not yet clear whether the battery-electric or range-extender version will reach local customers first.

The two powertrain options also give the G9L an unusually broad group of potential rivals. Its battery-electric versions will line up against large three-row EVs including the Kia EV9, Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90, while the range-extender may appeal to buyers considering plug-in hybrid SUVs such as the BYD Sealion 8. At the more affordable end of the range, mainstream large SUVs such as the Toyota Kluger and Hyundai Palisade could also be in the frame.

XPeng is pitching the G9L as a premium model, with European specifications featuring a large central touchscreen, rear entertainment screen and extensive seating comfort equipment. Australian features and pricing will be confirmed closer to launch.

The G9L will be another step in XPeng’s factory-backed Australian expansion, following the updated G6, X9 people mover and L03. While more models are expected to follow, the company has not yet detailed the next Australian launch beyond the G9L.

The post XPeng G9L SUV Australian pricing looms: Flagship SUV targets early 2027 showroom arrival appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Fancy an electric wagon? Mercedes-Benz CLA Shooting Brake electric priced at $72,990 for Australia, just $790 above sedan
data.description:
Mercedes-Benz has priced its electric CLA Shooting Brake for Australia at $72,990 before on-road costs, putting the wagon just $790 above the equivalent CLA 200 electric sedan.

Orders for the CLA 200 Shooting Brake electric open on October 22, with the first vehicles expected in Australian showrooms in January 2027.

The small premium over the $72,200 sedan buys a longer roofline, a large rear tailgate and more headroom, offering another option for EV buyers seeking practicality without moving into an SUV.

READ MORE: Best luxury EVs in Australia 2026: Premium electric cars under $100k, $150k, $250k and beyond, priced and compared

READ MORE: Mazda 6e and Mercedes-Benz CLA score five stars: So why isn’t ANCAP making a bigger deal about it?
READ MORE: 2026 Mercedes-Benz CLA electric Review: 800V tech and impressive range land Merc back in the EV fight
READ MORE: Mercedes-Benz GLA EV deep-dive: Just how much does it share with the new Mercedes-Benz CLA EV

The Shooting Brake will initially be offered here with one electric powertrain, combining a rear-mounted motor producing 165kW and 335Nm with a two-speed transmission and rear-wheel drive.

Mercedes-Benz claims a WLTP driving range of up to 511km, depending on specification, and electricity consumption of 13.2kWh/100km.

The Australian release lists an 800-volt electrical architecture, DC fast charging at up to 320kW under optimal conditions and AC charging at up to 22kW. It does not specify battery capacity or a 10-80 per cent charging time.

Navigation can incorporate charging stops into a journey and precondition the battery before arrival at a fast charger to help it reach the appropriate temperature for charging.

The two-speed gearbox uses its lower ratio for acceleration and its higher ratio to improve efficiency at speed. Mercedes-Benz also quotes regenerative braking of up to 200kW.

The electric Shooting Brake has a 455-litre rear luggage compartment and a separate 101-litre storage area beneath the bonnet.

Folding the rear seats increases rear cargo capacity to as much as 1290 litres, while the 40:20:40 split allows longer items to be carried with passengers still occupying the outer rear seats.

An electric tailgate with hands-free opening is standard. Mercedes-Benz says larger rear door openings improve access, while rear headroom increases by 26mm compared with the sedan. Front headroom grows by 14mm.

Standard equipment includes AMG Line styling, 18-inch alloy wheels, a panoramic glass roof, privacy glass, heated front seats, wireless phone charging, smartphone integration and a 360-degree camera.

Adaptive cruise control and blind-spot assistance are also included, along with the latest MBUX infotainment and Mercedes-Benz Operating System, which supports over-the-air updates.

The steering wheel brings back physical controls for cruise-control functions and audio volume, a change Mercedes-Benz says responds to customer feedback.

A $2850 Premium Package adds a head-up display, Burmester audio, upgraded headlights, a front-passenger screen and upgraded climate control. A Sport Package costs $1200, the Winter Package is $400 and switchable panoramic roof glass adds $1600.

The most obvious incoming rival is the Zeekr 7GT, another electric shooting brake headed for Australia. Its larger body and choice of rear- and all-wheel-drive powertrains broaden the comparison, although Australian pricing has yet to be officially announced.

Other electric wagons, including the BMW i5 M60 xDrive Touring and Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo, sit substantially further upmarket. That leaves the CLA with relatively little direct competition from established luxury brands at this price.

Buyers considering electric sedans and liftbacks could also cross-shop the Tesla Model 3, BYD Seal and BMW i4, although none offers the CLA Shooting Brake’s wagon body.

Mercedes-Benz will also offer a CLA 200 Shooting Brake petrol mild-hybrid at $70,800 before on-road costs, just $2190 below the EV. It combines a 1.5-litre four-cylinder engine with a 48-volt hybrid system, an eight-speed dual-clutch transmission and front-wheel drive.

The post Fancy an electric wagon? Mercedes-Benz CLA Shooting Brake electric priced at $72,990 for Australia, just $790 above sedan appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Tesla Cybertruck officially axed for Australia: Deposits refunded seven years after orders opened
data.description:
It’s official: the Tesla Cybertruck is not coming to Australia.

Tesla has today written to Australians and New Zealanders who reserved the stainless steel electric ute, confirming its plans to build a right-hand drive version have been scrapped.

An email sent this morning (Friday, October 23, 2026) finally put the full stop on any chances for the radical American pick-up truck, as many had expected.

READ MORE: Tesla bounces back with record Q2 deliveries: But what’s going on with the share price?
READ MORE: Tesla axes pricing! Plummeting Cybertruck sales prompt huge discounts
READ MORE: Local Tesla boss predicts Cybertruck could come to Australia as early as 2026
READ MORE: “It was never off the table”: Tesla Australia briefed on ADR requirements to launch Cybertruck as electric beast firms for our market
READ MORE: Tesla Cybertruck driven! Behind the wheel of the outlandish truck that Elon built
READ MORE: 2026 Tesla Model 3 Rear-Wheel Drive Brief Drive: Is the cheapest Tesla now the smartest buy?

“After careful consideration, plans to produce Cybertruck for Australia and New Zealand have been discontinued,” the email reads.

Reservations will be cancelled and deposits refunded in full. Customers will receive a separate email to confirm their refund details, after which Tesla says the money will be returned within 30 days.

There’s also a consolation prize of sorts. Those who reserved a Cybertruck are being offered a complimentary one-year Full Self-Driving (Supervised) subscription if they order a new Model 3 or Model Y, which can be combined with Tesla’s current offers.

FSD (Supervised currently costs $149 per month, so the offer is theoretically valued at $1788 – if you stump up $50K-plus for a new Tesla…

The Aussie demise of the Cybertruck – not that it ever got off the ground – ends a saga that has dragged on for almost seven years.

Australians were able to put down a $150 deposit for the Cybertruck from late 2019, shortly after the polarising pick-up was revealed. Tesla has previously said tens of thousands of Aussies placed reservations between 2019 and 2021.

The local reservation page was pulled in May 2022 and replaced with a “Get Updates” button, but deposits were never automatically refunded, leaving buyers in limbo.

Some asked for their money back in the meantime, which was granted as per the terms and conditions of the original deposits.

Tesla then imported evaluation Cybertrucks from 2024, taking them on a national roadshow and displaying them at motor shows and events.

Of course, there was a time when there was some hope the Cybertruck could make its way Down Under.

As recently as March 2025, Tesla Australia and New Zealand country director Thom Drew told EV Central he was “personally confident” the Cybertruck would come here, suggesting it could arrive as early as 2026.

Within a month, he was more cautious, telling us: “I am not confident it’s coming, but we are discussing it.”

By May 2025 the local team had been briefed on the Australian Design Rule changes needed, with Drew saying the required tweaks included bumper widths, external lighting and – obviously – the switch to right-hand drive.

But compliance was arguably never the biggest hurdle.

The sticking point was always the business case, with Australia likely to be the only right-hand drive market for a machine that hasn’t sold in anything like the numbers expected in America (turns out Americans love their traditional pick-up trucks from Chevrolet, Ram, Ford and Toyota).

Drew also conceded the large pick-up segment alone – which accounts for about 10,000 sales per year in Australia – wouldn’t be enough; he said the brand would look to lure buyers from large SUVs as well if it sold the Cybertruck here.

“If that was our only target segment I wouldn’t be advocating for it,” he said at the time.

Price was always a massive Cybertruck hurdle

Other than the stainless steel exoskeleton – which means it doesn’t need a separate chassis underneath – the Cybertruck was challenged by price.

In the US the dual-motor Cybertruck sells for around US$80,000 (Tesla initially promised it would kick off for half that price), which translates to roughly $130,000 here before on-road costs and local taxes.

While it would have been classified as a commercial vehicle – sidestepping the controversial luxury car tax – it would still have been a big ask in a market where full-size American pick-ups are a niche.

The Cybertruck also hasn’t sold in the numbers originally expected in the US, despite the enormous number of reservations taken before launch.

Tesla hasn’t publicly explained the decision beyond the email to customers.

For Aussies wanting an electrified ute, the market has moved on regardless, with plug-in hybrids such as the BYD Shark 6 and GWM Cannon Alpha, and fully electric options such as the new MG U9 EV, now on sale.

data.title: Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program
data.description:
Hyundai is preparing a new generation of cheaper, faster-charging and longer-lasting batteries to underpin a massive global product offensive that will see more than 100 new or updated vehicles launched by the end of the decade.

The Korean auto giant has detailed an extensive battery development program that includes new in-house battery cells, a switch to significantly cheaper mid-nickel chemistry for upcoming EVs, smarter battery management and new technology designed to prevent thermal runaway spreading through a battery pack.

It comes as Hyundai prepares one of the largest product rollouts in its history, with more than 100 global launches and major model updates planned by 2030.

READ MORE: Revealed: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute tech will debut in Santa Fe SUV range extender
READ MORE: Hyundai Ioniq 3 priced: UK version of new EV rival for BYD and MG starts at $42,500 … that’s promising for Australia
READ MORE: Hyundai’s 1000km-plus electric ute delayed: It’s still coming to Australia but it could take until 2030 to get here

More than 18 will take Hyundai into new products or market segments and seven new vehicles are due within the next eight months alone.

The rollout will include conventional combustion-powered vehicles, hybrids, extended-range electric vehicles (EREVs) and battery-electric vehicles, with electrified models targeted to account for 60 per cent of Hyundai sales by 2030, up from 23 per cent in 2025.

Hyundai is targeting 5.55 million global vehicle sales and a six per cent global market share by the end of the decade.

Central to the technology push is Hyundai’s development of its own battery cells.

The company claims its new high-performance cells can produce more than twice the output of the high-nickel cells it has previously used while reducing charging time by 40 per cent.

The first application will be Hyundai’s new EREV powertrain arriving in the first half of 2027.

That system will initially appear in the new Santa Fe EREV, which Hyundai says will offer more than 600 miles – about 965km – of total driving range.

Hyundai says the EREV requires less than half the battery capacity of a comparable battery-electric vehicle while still providing equivalent battery performance and EV driving characteristics.

The technology is also significant for Australia because EREV is emerging as a leading candidate to power Hyundai’s upcoming body-on-frame midsize ute.

But Hyundai’s battery plans extend well beyond EREVs.

One of the biggest developments for conventional battery-electric vehicles will arrive from 2027.

Hyundai says EVs launching next year will adopt mid-nickel NCM – nickel-cobalt-manganese – battery cells that will reduce battery costs by around 30 per cent compared with the technology they replace.

Importantly, Hyundai claims the cheaper cells will maintain what it describes as “optimal performance” under real-world driving conditions.

The potential significance is substantial because the battery remains one of the most expensive individual components in an electric vehicle.

A 30 per cent reduction in battery cost does not mean the price of an entire Hyundai EV will fall by 30 per cent, but reducing the cost of the pack potentially gives the company much greater scope to lower vehicle prices – or fit larger batteries and more equipment without pushing prices higher.

It should also help Hyundai compete against the rapidly expanding number of lower-cost Chinese EV manufacturers.

The first models using the new mid-nickel batteries have not been identified.

However, they will arrive during an enormous expansion of Hyundai’s electrified range.

In Europe alone Hyundai plans to cover 85 per cent of the market with a fully electrified portfolio, including five new SUVs and light-commercial vehicles, while increasing annual EV sales from 116,000 in 2025 to more than 420,000 by 2030.

Hyundai isn’t concentrating purely on the chemistry inside the battery.

Software will increasingly be used to manage the battery throughout its working life.

Hyundai says an enhanced cloud-based battery management system (BMS) will extend the average life of its EV batteries by 20 per cent by 2028.

The system will monitor battery condition and use cloud connectivity to detect abnormalities in individual cells in real time.

That could have implications beyond how long owners can keep their cars.

Battery degradation and the cost of replacing an EV battery remain important considerations for used EV buyers, while improved battery longevity potentially increases residual values and extends the useful life of an electric vehicle.

Hyundai hasn’t detailed exactly how it has calculated its claimed 20 per cent average battery-life improvement or translated it into expected kilometres or years of service.

The other major component of Hyundai’s battery strategy is safety.

Hyundai has developed what it calls Thermal Runaway Protection (TRP), designed to prevent heat from a failing battery cell spreading into adjacent cells.

Thermal runaway occurs when a battery cell experiences an uncontrolled increase in temperature that can trigger further cells, potentially creating a chain reaction within the battery pack.

Rather than simply delaying the spread of heat, Hyundai claims its TRP system can block it at the source.

It combines a battery design that dissipates heat with barriers between individual cells intended to stop heat transfer.

Hyundai says the technology has been verified through more than 200 repeated tests using both prismatic and pouch-type NCM batteries.

The cloud-based BMS and TRP effectively provide two layers of defence.

The BMS is intended to detect abnormal behaviour early enough for preventative action to be taken, while TRP provides a physical defence against heat spreading if a cell does fail.

The new thermal-runaway technology will make its production debut with Genesis, with Hyundai’s roadmap identifying the upcoming electric GV90 flagship SUV as its first application.

The battery investment is part of a broader change in Hyundai’s electrification strategy.

Rather than relying exclusively on battery-electric vehicles, Hyundai is expanding across EVs, hybrids and EREVs as it pushes towards its 5.55-million annual sales target.

Among the models identified in the latest roadmap are the IONIQ 3, new-generation Tucson and Tucson Hybrid, Santa Fe EREV, a new electric SUV for India and new global and European B-segment SUVs.

Genesis will simultaneously expand beyond pure EVs with its first hybrid, the GV80 Hybrid, as well as an EREV SUV targeting more than 640 miles – around 1030km – of total range and the battery-electric GV90 flagship.

The post Hyundai’s battery breakthrough: Next-gen tech will back massive 100-model global launch program appeared first on EV Central.

data.title: Look out Toyota RAV4: Omoda X is another Chinese SUV coming for your customers. And it’s an EV!
data.description:
Omoda Jaecoo has revealed a new Toyota RAV4-sized SUV with electric and plug-in hybrid power, rugged styling and a night-vision camera designed to spot hazards after dark.

Called the Omoda X, the concept made its global debut at parent company Chery’s International User Summit in Wuhu, China, on October 20.

It shapes as another potential entrant in Australia’s crowded medium SUV market, although Omoda Jaecoo has yet to confirm a local launch, timing or pricing.

READ MORE: Striking Chery Omoda 4 is a baby Lamborghini Urus built for Australian tastes: Chinese brand chases the BYD Atto 2 and Kia EV3
READ MORE: 2025 Omoda 9 Review: New premium plug-in hybrid takes the fight to Tesla, BYD, Zeekr, Mazda, Volvo – and more
READ MORE: Omoda, Jaecoo the latest new Chinese brands to take on BYD, GWM, Deepal, Zeekr, Leapmotor and XPeng

The X sits below the Omoda 9 and measures 4650mm long, 1910mm wide and 1720mm tall, putting it firmly in the family SUV territory occupied by the RAV4.

Omoda has confirmed plans for both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains, along with two-wheel drive and all-wheel drive options. It has not detailed which combinations will be offered, or released battery capacities, driving ranges, charging specifications or power and torque outputs.

Instead, the reveal has focused on a tougher design and equipment intended to give the X appeal beyond the suburban school run.

Omoda claims 200mm of ground clearance, a wading depth of more than 700mm and a towing capacity of up to 1800kg. The roof has a stated load capacity of 75kg, while the reveal vehicle rides on 19-inch alloy wheels with all-terrain tyres.

The angular body features pronounced wheelarches, extensive protective-looking cladding and distinctive front and rear lighting. Omoda describes the styling as inspired by “mecha” culture, continuing the robot-like design themes of its newer models.

One feature with particular relevance to Australian country roads is an infrared thermal imaging night-vision system, a first for Omoda Jaecoo.

The company says it can identify potential hazards up to 90 metres away. Its ability to detect animals could be useful where wildlife is difficult to see at night, although its effectiveness in Australian conditions remains to be assessed.

Other features shown at the reveal include a panoramic glass roof claimed to reduce cabin temperatures in sunlight by seven degrees Celsius, and a scratch-resistant, self-healing clearcoat called ProGloss Plus.

Inside, the X combines a 10.25-inch digital instrument cluster with a 13.2-inch central touchscreen, a twin-wing dashboard layout and an X-shaped floating centre console.

Physical switches and rotary controls operate frequently used functions, including the air-conditioning and driving modes, while Omoda claims 39 storage spaces throughout the cabin.

A configurable X-Mode allows drivers to tailor vehicle settings and responses. The cabin technology also includes a conversational voice assistant and a karaoke system that uses four microphone zones, allowing occupants to sing along without handheld microphones.

For now, Omoda Jaecoo’s confirmed Australian expansion includes the Omoda 4 and Omoda 7, both due in the first half of 2027 after their local unveiling at Everything Electric Sydney in September.

The post Look out Toyota RAV4: Omoda X is another Chinese SUV coming for your customers. And it’s an EV! appeared first on EV Central.
